 search results for “cruise itinerary sample” and “cruise ship itinerary sample” usually want a readable pattern, not a marketing list of ports
the table below is a  generic educational sample , not a named sailing
real routes replace “port a / port b” with published calls
always use the line’s final itinerary for all-aboard times

day  typical pattern  what to plan  
 
 
  1  embarkation  arrive early enough for security and mandatory muster
2  sea day  full ship day: dining, shows, pools, and recovery from travel
3  port day (full call)  one main activity plus buffer to be back well before all aboard
4  port day (shorter call)  stay closer to the terminal
skip stacked tours that need a long transfer
5  sea day  rest after two port days
use the ship instead of forcing another excursion
6  port day  if the call is scenic cruising plus a late arrival, keep plans flexible
7  sea day or last port  pack overnight bags, settle onboard accounts, and confirm disembarkation instructions
8  disembarkation  leave according to the line’s groups
build extra time for flights—do not book the first departure of the morning unless the line says it is safe
shorter 3–5 night cruises often drop a sea day
transatlantic and repositioning cruises invert the sample: more consecutive sea days, fewer ports
browse  ship guides  and  port guides  together so the ship and the route match

how to read a sample itinerary 
 
  embarkation day is not a port day
you are boarding, clearing security, and finding your cabin
published hours ashore are shorter than they look
subtract tendering, walking to the gate, and the buffer before all aboard
two long port days in a row  is a common way first-timers get exhausted
put a sea day between them when you can choose
repeat ports  on longer voyages can be useful (second neighborhood, second meal) or redundant

sea days vs port days 
   
 sea days mean the ship does not call at a port
port days mean you can go ashore, subject to the terminal, tenders, and immigration
a typical 7-night  caribbean  loop might include one or two sea days
a transatlantic crossing can string six or seven sea days together
for the rest-versus-exploration tradeoff, read  port days vs sea days

region and season 
   
   caribbean :  winter and spring are peak; late summer and fall overlap hurricane season
mediterranean:  spring and fall are often more comfortable than mid-summer crowds
norwegian fjords:  long summer daylight, cooler weather, and scenic cruising between calls
season also changes port hours and tender likelihood
use seadays port pages for terminal notes on specific calls—do not assume every “7-night” product uses the same piers

port duration, excursions, and rushed days 
   
 short calls (often in the 4–6 hour range) suit a walk, one nearby sight, or staying onboard
longer calls can support a proper tour—if the transfer time is realistic
book independent tours only with a buffer that would still get you back if traffic or tenders run late
families should treat kids-club hours, nap windows, and accessibility as itinerary constraints, not afterthoughts
a “perfect” port list that requires sprinting every morning is the wrong sample for that group

embarkation, disembarkation, and repositioning 
   
 the start and end ports affect total cost as much as the fare: flights, hotels, and transfers
repositioning cruises often look cheap because they include many sea days and one-way geography—budget the extra flight before you call it a deal

a sea day is exactly what it sounds like: a full day when your cruise ship stays at sea instead of docking at a port

on port days, half the ship is gone
on sea days, everything is open and ready

           the real cost of cruise drink packages: is it worth it

published by seadays 
             apr 8, 2026

 what a drink package actually is 
 a cruise drink package is a prepaid beverage plan sold by the cruise line
most mainstream packages cover a defined list of drinks up to a per-drink cap
soda-only, non-alcoholic, and beer-and-wine plans are separate products
this page is about deciding whether any package beats paying as you go —not about naming a current price, which changes by line, sailing, and promotion

get seadays          
 always read the current terms for your booking
packages can exclude bottled water brands, fresh juices, specialty coffee, room-service drinks, or drinks above a posted limit
related:  port days vs sea days: how to balance exploration, rest, and onboard fun  ·  is unlimited food on cruises really unlimited

what the buffets don’t advertise  ·  how to save money on shore excursions without missing out  ·  cruise ship operations: what happens behind the scenes   the only math that matters 
 a package is worth it when your  expected prepaid-covered drinks would cost more à la carte than the package, after taxes

use this break-even sketch (plug in  your  sailing’s numbers): 
 
 package price per person, per day (or voyage total ÷ days)
typical covered drink price onboard, including the auto-if it is added per drink
drinks per person per day you will actually order from the covered list—not the number you wish you would order
if (drinks × à la carte price) is below the daily package price, paying as you go wins
if you routinely exceed that, the package can win
seadays has a dedicated walkthrough of that arithmetic in  the seadays drink package calculator math  and a “loses money” view in  when the beverage package actually loses money

who it usually helps 
 
 guests who order several covered alcoholic drinks every sea day and port evening
guests who would buy specialty coffee or mocktails all day on a soda/non-alcoholic plan that actually covers those items
sailings where à la carte prices are high and the package is on a genuine pre-cruise discount—not a “discount” off an inflated onboard rate

who it usually does not help 
 
 light drinkers, or anyone who mostly drinks included water, iced tea, and dining-room coffee
guests who go ashore most days and drink on land (packages do not follow you into  port )
anyone who will not use the package on embarkation afternoon or disembarkation morning—those half-days still count as full days on many plans
cabins where the line requires  every adult  to buy the same alcoholic package
one heavy drinker cannot subsidize three light drinkers

hidden costs people miss 
 on packages can be a daily add-on rather than included
some lines charge a daily even if you barely drink
specialty dining pairings, bottled wine at dinner, and souvenir glasses are often outside the package
if you care about wine at dinner, compare a bottle’s onboard price to several package pours—not to a restaurant on land
alcoholic packages are for guests who meet the line’s drinking age (21 on most ships calling on the us; 18 on some other itineraries)
do not assume a teen soda package equals an adult plan

how to decide before you buy 
 
 list what you drank on your last vacation, honestly
open the line’s current package inclusions for your sailing dates
run the break-even with the seadays calculator articles above, or the in-app  drink package calculator
if you are within a drink or two of break-even, skip the package
unused prepaid drinks are a worse outcome than one extra à la carte cocktail
seadays does not sell drink packages and does not invent onboard menus
keep the decision next to your budget in the  cruise budget planner

          what the shipping emissions data actually says 
   
 the widely quoted greenhouse-gas study for ships is about shipping, not a cruise-passenger footprint

the fourth imo ghg study 2020, summarized on the international maritime organization’s site, estimates greenhouse-gas emissions from total shipping (international, domestic, and fishing) at 977 million tonnes in 2012 and 1,076 million tonnes in 2018
it puts shipping’s share of global anthropogenic emissions at 2.76% in 2012 and 2.89% in 2018
those tonnes are not “cruises.” they include cargo ships

get seadays          
 the same study’s executive summary says container ships, cruise ships, and oil tankers have a smaller share of their own emissions in the phase it defines as cruising, because those ships spend more time slow or near port

it does not say a cruise holiday is a small part of your personal emissions, and it does not publish a single percentage for “cruise ships cause x% of global co₂.” if a page gives you that percentage without a table, it invented it

related:  the rise of digital nomads on cruise ships: hype, reality, and wifi economics  ·  the truth about cruise ship internet: speed test results, myths, and what to expect  ·  cruise ship design: how do they stay afloat (and why they're so big)
·  the real cost of cruise drink packages: is it worth it
days at sea and days in port change how a ship runs
the imo point about time near port is a fleet pattern, not a reason to skip or book a particular call
some lines publish fuel, shore-power, and wastewater figures for a year
do not mix a 2018 global inventory with a 2026 brochure
a ship plugged in at a pier is not burning the same way as a ship running generators
whether your port offers it is a port and ship question
look at the port authority or the line’s call sheet, not a generic “green cruise” label

emissions are not the sewage rules 
 the imo greenhouse-gas study counts gases
it is not the rulebook for garbage or sewage
those sit in marpol, the same organization’s pollution convention
a page that quotes the 2.89% shipping share and then tells you whether your ship dumps waste is using the wrong document
for waste, start at the imo’s marpol pages and then the cruise line’s environmental report for the year you are sailing
passenger behavior is the small part you control: use the bins the ship labels, do not throw anything over the side, and do not treat a “green” marketing line as a measurement
the measurement, when it exists, is in the line’s report or in the imo inventory, with a year attached

what this article will not claim 
 it will not rank cruise lines by cleanliness

it will not convert the imo tonnes into “your week equals x flights.” that conversion needs assumptions about occupancy, fuel, and the flights you would have taken, and this page does not have those assumptions from a source that covers your sailing
if you want a number for a decision, start with the imo totals so you know the scale of all shipping, then read the cruise line’s latest environmental report for the fleet you are actually booking
putting them in one sentence without saying so is how bad cruise-environment articles get written
check the date on whichever pdf you open
a line’s report is usually a later year and a smaller fleet
neither number updates itself because the article title says 2026
figures are the imo study’s, for total shipping, through 2018

mid-ship cabins on lower decks tend to have less motion, which can help babies sleep better
sea days are usually the easiest days with infants because there is no pressure to leave the ship
you can build your own rhythm around naps, meals, and quiet time
port days, on the other hand, may require more planning, especially when it comes to transportation, weather, and walking distances
for first-time family cruises with infants, shorter itineraries (3–5 nights) are often a better starting point
best cruises for kids (ages 4–12)     this is where cruising really shines for families
kids between 4 and 12 usually find cruise ships incredibly exciting because there is always something happening

the best cruise ships for this age group include:    supervised kids clubs with structured activities  water parks, slides, and splash zones  themed events and character experiences  interactive games and competitions  family-friendly shows and performances   kids clubs are one of the biggest advantages of cruising
these clubs group children by age and offer activities throughout the day, from arts and crafts to games and mini competitions
this allows kids to make new friends while parents get some time to relax
sea days are typically packed with activities for kids, making them one of the highlights of the trip
from pool games to treasure hunts, there’s rarely a dull moment
buffets and casual dining options make it simple to find food that kids enjoy, even for picky eaters
best cruises for teens     teenagers need a completely different cruise experience

they want independence, social interaction, and activities that don’t feel “too young.”   the best cruise ships for teens offer:    dedicated teen lounges or hangout zones  gaming rooms and vr experiences  sports courts and fitness areas  organized meetups and social events  •music, parties, and late-night activities   one of the biggest benefits of cruising for teens is the balance between freedom and safety
teens can explore the ship, meet others their age, and participate in activities — all within a controlled environment
however, not all ships are equally appealing to teens
smaller or older ships may have fewer options, which can lead to boredom
that’s why choosing a ship with strong teen programming is key
sea days again play an important role here, as they give teens more time to socialize and explore the ship
choosing the right cabin for families     cabin choice can significantly impact your cruise experience, especially with children
while it might be tempting to choose the cheapest option, space and layout matter more when traveling as a family

cruise cabins are compact, so having enough room for luggage, strollers, and daily items helps keep things organized
for families with younger children, being close to key areas like dining and kids clubs can make daily routines much easier
planning the perfect family cruise  a great family cruise doesn’t happen by accident — it comes down to planning

before booking, it’s helpful to think about:    cruise length (shorter for first trips, longer for experienced travelers)  balance between sea days and port days  destinations that are family-friendly  onboard activities for different age groups  dining flexibility and options   it’s also worth planning your daily schedule loosely, especially on sea days
having a rough idea of activities, shows, and meals helps avoid unnecessary stress
many families also like to track their cruise history, ships, and itineraries over time

          do cruise ships run out of food
large cruise ships do not operate like a café that can sell the last sandwich and close
they provision for the voyage with a buffer, then cook in cycles
guests are not expected to skip dinner because the ship “ran out of food.” that is not how hotel operations on a passenger ship are planned

get seadays          
 what  does  happen is more specific: a particular dish, pastry, ice-cream flavor, or specialty-restaurant item can sell out for a meal period
a weather delay can postpone a scheduled provision call
a dietary request that was never filed can be hard to fill at 9 p.m
those are shortages of  a choice , not of calories

how provisioning actually works 
 food and hotel stores are loaded before departure, sized for passenger and crew counts plus extra days
many itineraries also take stores in a turnaround port
exact menus, brands, and quantities are line- and sailing-specific
on  sea days  the galley is still producing breakfast, lunch, dinner, and late-night options
on  port days  some venues reduce hours because many guests are ashore—not because the ship has no food

what can sell out 
 
 a featured dessert, a limited sushi roll, or a steak temperature in a specialty restaurant at a popular seating
a brunch item toward the end of buffet service
room-service hours or a specific cabin-menu item during peak disembarkation morning
a “market” or extra-cost café pastry after a rush
if a dish is gone, ask which other included venue is open
that is not guaranteed on every ship at every hour
ask dining staff rather than assuming the ship has stopped feeding people

special diets and allergies 
 most large lines can handle common allergies and diets when you tell them  before or at the start of the sailing , not at the buffet sneeze-guard
if a request is complex, speak with the dining room on embarkation day

practical takeaways 
 
 you will not starve on a mainstream cruise because the ship “ran out of food.” 
 you might miss one item you wanted
use your  cruise planner  so dining times and specialty bookings are not last-minute
room-service and extra-cost venues can pause or limit items even when the main dining room is fully open

 cabin types, not “best rooms” 
   
 cruise lines sell the same four cabin families on most large ships:  inside  (no window),  oceanview  (window or porthole),  balcony  (private veranda), and  suite  (more space and extra service that varies by line)

they work well if you are rarely in the room except to sleep and change
they are a poor fit if you want a view, natural light, or a sitting area

oceanview cabins 
 oceanview cabins add a window or porthole
some are obstructed by lifeboats or metalwork—those are usually cheaper and should be labeled
a window does not give you outdoor space
if the view matters more than stepping outside, oceanview can be the value pick versus a balcony

balcony cabins 
 a balcony adds private outdoor space
downsides: higher fare, more motion on high/forward/aft decks in a seaway, and furniture that can be wet or windy
on cold or repositioning itineraries you may barely use it
on warm  port-intensive itineraries  many guests use the balcony every morning
others add a separate living area, extra attendants, or included extras (dining, laundry, or lounge access)
do not assume a “suite” includes drinks, wi‑fi, or specialty dining unless the fare code says so

locations that commonly disappoint 
 these patterns show up across many ships

they are not a rating of any one vessel: 
 
  under the pool deck, buffet, or lido:  early-morning furniture dragging, late-night music, and kids running overhead
near theaters, clubs, or the casino:  show let-out noise and bass through bulkheads
aft can feel vibration from propulsion on some ships
connecting-cabin doors:  extra noise if the other cabin is occupied by strangers
guarantee / “choice of” categories:  you get the cabin type, not a chosen location
fine if you are flexible; risky if you need midship or a quiet deck

locations that are often quieter 
 midship, on a cabin-only deck (cabins above and below), away from stairs and elevators, is the usual quiet/motion compromise
that is a tendency, not a promise: a cabin under a galley or laundry can still be noisy

what to check before you book 
 
 open the deck plan and look one deck above and below your category

search the category code for “obstructed,” “metal structures,” or “partial view.” 
 if anyone in the party is motion-sensitive, prefer midship and avoid the highest forward cabins
if you share a cabin, decide closet and outlet needs before buying extras
see the  cruise packing list  and  what to assign before a second power strip
pair cabin choice with  first-time cruise tips  so embarkation and dining are not afterthoughts

accessible and family cabins 
 accessible cabins are limited and must match the guest’s documented needs
family cabins (pullmans, sofa beds, connecting pairs) sell out early on school-holiday sailings
book those as named cabins, not guarantees, if the layout matters
seadays does not assign cabins and does not publish invented occupancy scores
use the line’s deck plan, then keep the choice in your  cruise planner  with the rest of the sailing

ai enters as decision support—routing optimization, predictive maintenance, demand forecasting for food and labor—more often than as a robot bartender headline

what the buffets don’t advertise   ai onboard—what helps guests vs what helps the back office     guest-facing ai today often means chat assistants in apps, translation tools, and recommendation engines for dining and shows

comparison: airlines use optimization math for fuel and crew legality; cruise lines add hotel scale and multiple kitchen venues per ship
practical insight : when an app suggests a restaurant, you are seeing revenue management plus personalization—helpful, but not neutral

smart ships vs smarter marketing  a  smart ship  claim should be unpackable: hull sensors
led hull lighting is fun, but it is not  the same  category as shore power hooks that cut emissions in port
example: two ships may both advertise “advanced efficiency,” but one reduces fuel burn with route optimization and waste heat recovery, while another primarily upgraded guest wifi radios

floating cities—useful metaphor, risky expectation  calling a mega-ship a floating city explains scale—neighborhoods, transit time, micro economies—but it can mislead guests into urban assumptions that do not hold
cities have hospitals with full specialties; ships have clinics optimized for stabilization
cities have competing isps; ships have satellite and radio constraints that cap real-world mbps
insight: treat mega-ships as dense resorts with maritime rules, not as duplicates of onshore life

mitigation: use privacy settings, avoid public wifi for sensitive tasks, and enable multifactor authentication on accounts tied to payments
insight: security habits on land still apply at sea—ship networks are managed, not magically safe
robotics and labor—what changes for crew  robots capture headlines, but crew value often moves up the skill stack: higher touch service, complex problem solving, safety leadership
automation in galleys may reduce repetitive strain; it does not remove human judgment during rough seas or allergen incidents
comparison: airport kiosks did not delete agents—they shifted where humans spend minutes
ports, infrastructure, and the network effect     smart ships only shine when ports coordinate berth power, waste offload, and transit flows

wearables, biometrics, and the queue-reduction wave     some lines experiment with wearables for payments and cabin entry, facial recognition for embarkation throughput, and apps that reserve shows to flatten lines

           what is a sea day on a cruise

published by seadays 
             mar 14, 2026 
             8 min read 
           
           
         
         
 what is a sea day on a cruise
a  sea day  is a day when the ship is underway and does not call at a port
the itinerary is still moving—often overnight between two ports, or across a stretch of open water that takes a full day or more

get seadays          
 sea days are the opposite of  port days , when the ship is alongside (or at anchor) and guests can go ashore
transatlantic and repositioning sailings can string several sea days together
the ship still runs on a published daily program: meals, activities, shows, and safety information
you do not “stop traveling” on a sea day; you travel while using the ship as the destination

what happens onboard 
 crew keep hotel, dining, and entertainment operations running

guests can use public spaces that may be quieter than on embarkation day: pools and sun decks (weather permitting), the buffet and main restaurants, the theater, gym, spa (often extra-cost), shops, and lounges
expect a daily planner—paper, cabin tv, or the line’s app—listing times for trivia, classes, kids clubs, and evening shows
exact offerings depend on the ship and sailing
do not assume every vessel has the same venues

a typical sea-day rhythm 
 schedules vary by line, but many guests fall into a loose pattern: 
 
  morning:  breakfast, a walk on deck, gym, or a quiet lounge with coffee
midday:  pool or indoor public rooms, lunch, and optional classes or spa appointments
afternoon:  reading, trivia, kids club pickup, or a nap before dinner
evening:  main dining or specialty restaurants, a production show or live music, then late-night lounges if you want them
some travelers treat a sea day as a full spa-and-show day

what passengers can do 
   
 common sea-day options, when the ship offers them: 
 
 pools, whirlpools, and sun decks (more crowded in warm weather and on the first sea day after embarkation)
main dining rooms, buffet, cafés, and extra-cost specialty restaurants
theater shows, live music, comedy, and movies—check the daily program
fitness classes and the gym; spa treatments are usually priced separately
kids and teen clubs on family-oriented ships, with age bands set by the line
some talks are sales presentations; read the description
for a longer activity list, see  sea day activities: what to do when you're not in port

family considerations 
 sea days can be easier than port days with young children: no all-aboard countdown, no tender queues, and clubs that often run fuller programs at sea
confirm age limits and signup rules on embarkation day
bring a simple cabin kit (sunscreen, light layers, a quiet activity) so you are not dependent on a single crowded pool

dining on a sea day 
 most lines keep included dining open on a similar schedule to port days
specialty restaurants may be easier to book at sea because fewer guests are ashore
if you care about a specific seating time, reserve early in the cruise rather than waiting for a sea day
dietary needs should be flagged with dining staff at the start of the sailing—not invented here as a ship-specific menu promise
a sea day removes shore logistics, which many guests find restful
the same day can feel busy if you stack trivia, a show, a specialty dinner, and a late lounge
crowds concentrate around the pool in good weather and around the buffet at peak meal times
if you want quiet, look for indoor lounges away from the pool deck and eat slightly off-peak
for a comparison of rest versus exploration, read  port days vs sea days

what to pack for sea days 
 you do not need a separate suitcase, but a few items make sea days smoother: 
 
 layers and a light jacket—open decks are windier than the cabin
reef-safe sunscreen and a hat if you plan to sit outside
a small bag for the spa or gym if you use them
motion-sickness precautions if you are sensitive; open water can feel different from a sheltered port approach
choose a midship, lower cabin if that is a concern, and follow your clinician’s advice—not generic internet dosages
see also  cruise packing list: what to bring and what to leave home

planning tips 
 
 read the next day’s program the night before so you are not deciding everything at breakfast
if the sailing has only one sea day, treat popular spa slots and specialty dining as limited—book early
keep ship time on your watch or phone
sea days still have show times and dinner seatings
use a sea day to rest before a long port day, or to catch up after a late-night arrival
track how many sea days you have actually sailed
the seadays app can log voyages, ships, and sea-day counts in one place

frequently asked questions 
 is a sea day the same as a day at sea
it means the ship is not scheduled to dock or tender guests ashore that day
can you get off the ship on a sea day
you remain onboard until the next scheduled arrival
check your daily program rather than assuming 24/7 access
some lines discount spa treatments on port days (when fewer guests are onboard) rather than on sea days
drink packages, wi-fi, and specialty dining follow the fare you already bought—not a special sea-day price list
how many sea days should a first-time cruiser look for
short caribbean loops may have one sea day or none
choose based on whether you want more time ashore or more time using the ship
browse  ship guides  and  port guides  together so the mix matches your trip
